# 1 Kings Chapter 7 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A)

---

**1** Solomon spent thirteen years building his own palace complex before it was completed.

**2** He built the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon — one hundred fifty feet long, seventy-five feet wide, and forty-five feet high — with four rows of cedar columns supporting cedar beams.

**3** It was roofed with cedar above the beams resting on the columns — forty-five beams, fifteen per row.

**4** There were three rows of windows with frames, each one facing a corresponding window opposite.

**5** All the doorways and windows had rectangular frames, set in matching rows of three.

**6** He made the Hall of Pillars — seventy-five feet long and forty-five feet wide — with a covered porch in front, supported by pillars.

**7** He built the Throne Hall — the Hall of Justice — where he would hear cases. It was paneled with cedar from floor to ceiling.

**8** His personal residence was set in another courtyard behind the hall, built in the same style. He also built a palace like the hall for Pharaoh's daughter, whom he had married.

**9** All these structures were made of premium stone blocks, precision-cut with saws on all sides, from foundation to roofline, and from the buildings out to the great courtyard.

**10** The foundations were of massive, expensive stone — blocks fifteen feet and twelve feet long.

**11** Above the foundation were more cut stones and cedar beams.

**12** The great courtyard was enclosed by three courses of cut stone and one course of cedar beams — the same construction used for the inner court of the LORD's temple and the temple vestibule.

**13** King Solomon sent for a craftsman named Hiram from Tyre.

**14** His mother was a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a Tyrian bronzeworker. Hiram was extraordinarily gifted — filled with skill, intelligence, and expertise in all kinds of bronze work. He came to King Solomon and carried out all his commissions.

**15** He cast two bronze pillars, each twenty-seven feet tall, with a circumference of eighteen feet.

**16** He made two bronze capitals to go on top of the pillars, each seven and a half feet tall.

**17** The capitals had lattice networks decorated with chain designs — seven chains for each capital.

**18** He made two rows of pomegranates around each network to cover the capitals on top of the pillars.

**19** The capitals on the pillars in the vestibule were shaped like lilies, six feet tall.

**20** On both capitals, above and next to the rounded section by the network, were two hundred pomegranates in rows all around.

**21** He erected the pillars at the entrance of the temple. The one on the right he named Jachin, and the one on the left he named Boaz.

**22** The tops of the pillars were shaped like lilies. And so the work on the pillars was completed.

**23** He then cast the Sea — a circular basin fifteen feet from rim to rim, seven and a half feet deep, and forty-five feet in circumference.

**24** Below the rim, two rows of gourds encircled it — ten gourds per foot and a half — cast as part of the basin.

**25** The Sea rested on twelve bronze bulls — three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east — with all their hindquarters pointing inward.

**26** The basin was three inches thick, with a rim shaped like a cup, like a lily blossom. It held about 12,000 gallons.

**27** He also made ten bronze stands, each six feet long, six feet wide, and four and a half feet tall.

**28** The stands were constructed with panels set between uprights.

**29** On the panels between the uprights were lions, bulls, and cherubim. On the uprights — above and below the lions and bulls — were wreaths of hammered work.

**30** Each stand had four bronze wheels with bronze axles. At its four corners were supports; beneath each basin were cast supports with wreaths on each side.

**31** Inside the stand, the opening was round — a pedestal rising eighteen inches above, set in a circular frame twenty-seven inches deep. The opening had engravings, and the frames were square, not round.

**32** The four wheels were under the panels. The wheel axles were attached to the stand, and each wheel was twenty-seven inches in diameter.

**33** The wheels were built like chariot wheels, with cast axles, rims, spokes, and hubs.

**34** There were four supports at the four corners of each stand, cast as one piece with the stand.

**35** On the top of each stand was a circular band nine inches high. The stays and panels on top were cast as one piece.

**36** He engraved the surfaces of the stays and panels with cherubim, lions, and palm trees wherever there was space, with wreaths all around.

**37** This is how he made all ten stands — each one identical in casting, size, and shape.

**38** He then made ten bronze basins, each holding about 240 gallons, each six feet across — one basin for each of the ten stands.

**39** He placed five stands on the south side of the temple and five on the north side. He set the Sea at the southeast corner.

**40** Hiram also made the pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls. So Hiram finished all the work he had undertaken for King Solomon in the temple of the LORD:

**41** the two pillars; the two bowl-shaped capitals on top of the pillars; the two sets of network covering the capitals;

**42** the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks — two rows of pomegranates for each network, covering the bowl-shaped capitals;

**43** the ten stands with their ten basins;

**44** the Sea with its twelve bulls underneath;

**45** the pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls. All these objects that Hiram made for King Solomon for the LORD's temple were of polished bronze.

**46** The king had them cast in clay molds in the Jordan Valley between Succoth and Zarethan.

**47** Solomon did not weigh any of these items because there were so many — the total weight of the bronze was beyond calculation.

**48** Solomon also made all the furnishings for the LORD's temple: the gold altar; the gold table for the bread of the Presence;

**49** the lampstands of pure gold — five on the right and five on the left in front of the inner sanctuary — with their gold flowers, lamps, and tongs;

**50** the pure gold cups, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, ladles, and censers; and the gold hinges for the doors of the inner sanctuary (the Most Holy Place) and for the doors of the main hall.

**51** When all the work King Solomon had done for the LORD's temple was finished, he brought in the items his father David had dedicated — the silver, the gold, and the furnishings — and placed them in the treasuries of the LORD's temple.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

1. **7:1 — thirteen years**: The narrator plants a quiet bomb. Solomon's palace took thirteen years; God's temple took seven. No commentary is offered. None is needed.

2. **7:14 — Hiram the artist**: This craftsman is described with the same language used for Bezalel, who built the tabernacle (Exod 31:3). He is "filled with wisdom, understanding, and expertise." The parallel is deliberate: the same Spirit that inspired the wilderness sanctuary now inspires its permanent successor.

3. **7:21 — Jachin and Boaz**: Two freestanding bronze pillars at the temple entrance, named "He establishes" and "In him is strength." They are not structural supports — they are theological declarations. Everyone entering the temple passes between them and their message.

4. **7:23-26 — the Sea**: A massive bronze basin holding thousands of gallons, resting on twelve bulls facing the four directions. This is not just a wash basin. It is a symbol of the cosmic waters — the chaotic deep (tehom) that God subdued at creation, now tamed and contained in the temple courtyard.

5. **7:47 — "beyond calculation"**: The amount of bronze used was so enormous it couldn't be weighed. This is extravagance as theology: what is given to God should exceed the capacity for measurement.

— PNEUMA
